A Time of War : A Memoir Across Three Generations

The air hangs heavy with the scent of gunpowder and fear. Across the continent, old alliances fracture as the Unified Monarchists and the Separatists clash for supremacy. Even in our quiet corner of the world, the drumbeat of war grows louder with every passing day.

Our father's work does not pause for the petty squabbles of kings and rebels, yet we cannot ignore the storm gathering at our doorstep. Whether we profit from the conflict or shield our estates from its fury, the choices we make in the coming years will echo across generations.
Taking Sides

Word has reached the village that armies are marching through the neighboring provinces. In the taverns and the Town Hall, whispers of espionage, conscription, and fortune-making dominate every conversation.

Representatives from both factions have been spotted in the region, each seeking coin, supplies, and loyalty. Soon, our village will be forced to declare where it stands.
War on the Horizon

A regiment of the {{0=warwinner}} has established an outpost near the border of our valley. Their scouts ride openly along the high roads, and their emissaries have already begun courting the local magistrate.

Though the outcome of this war is far from certain, the presence of the {{0=warwinner}} has emboldened their sympathizers in town while driving their rivals into the shadows.

Plagued by Conflict

If one can call the prospect of perpetual conflict stabilizing, my life settled into a somewhat steady routine. During the day, the sound of distant gunfire rumbled through the halls of my estate as silver plumes of smoke billowed beyond the mountainous horizon, casting tendril-like shadows across the land — a constant reminder of civil war. At night, the rare spectacle of an explosion brightening the sky surprised me with how viscerally I reacted.

Soldiers in their bright regalia keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost, waving the brilliant orange flag of royalty. The Monarchy had claimed victory from afar after stationing their ranks across the region, but as scuffles remained constant, this declaration was all pomp without substance. The Monarchy drafted citizens into their ranks and levied penalties against those who showed disloyalty.

The inference that one of my standing should owe a debt of servitude to those who already tax my earnings into oblivion was enough to make me spill my tea. And to what end, I wondered? Could peace be mustered in a populace kept so distant from the individuals who ruled it? It was called the industrial revolution for a reason, was it not?

But, I must admit, the safety that the Monarchy afforded appealed to my pocketbook. Appeasing the Monarchy would ensure money and influence, but it also appeared — for better or ill — that royalty was distant enough to take little interest in our experimentations unless they provided direct benefit to themselves, whereas the Separatists were interested in knowledge and were desperate to explore all scientific options available to them to turn the tide. However, their frail sensibilities would not so easily accept my experimentations.

Ah, to be left to one's own devices or to be famously scrutinized, reviled, and revered in equal measure! The decision weighed upon me so heavily it gave me mild indigestion during my evening banquets. What direction should I choose to advance my most important scientific work?
Down with the Monarchy

The length and difficulty of my journey was exacerbated by the ongoing conflict. Compounding this harried inconvenience, my spouse and I suffered the indignity of a lengthy interrogation by soldiers of the Separatist forces, who had imposed an unofficial martial government.

Peasants-turned-soldiers in their motley uniforms keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost waving a sanguine flag. A New Generation

And thus passed an entire generation under the yolk of constant battle and misery. Even after the Separatists claimed victory, skirmishes broke out within the land between the loyalists to the crown and the angry separatists.

Over the years, the rebel leaders were able to establish a fragile democratic coalition in the region, especially after making the family's town a center for scientific and industrial progress. Through their tireless work, the town's monarchist sympathies faded to a memory as they realized their freedom was tied intimately with the new republic.

By the time our hero's heir inherited the estate, a vibrant period of ambitious rebuilding returned to the town and surrounding countryside. Yet across the borders, the deposed Monarch's allies gathered their armies to crush the young republic.

Unfortunately, their heirs had been granted a much larger piece of the estate to manage. In fact, all of it. Every cousin's child was named an equal successor to the same plots of land in a mad scheme written into all of the wills simultaneously. It felt almost as if they were being watched and toyed with by an unseen spectral adversary.

Behind the Curve

My close friends and family - many of whom I have permanently severed contact with because of their feelings on the matter - have expressed extreme misgivings about the publication of this book. They claim that my macabre fascination with exposing this to the world is unhealthy!

Some have even derisively labeled this work as pseudoscience, homeopathy, or a drug-induced fever dream, but I say to them, "who are you to criticize the moon and the stars for being in the sky?" This work is important! How can they not see it? If anything, these outlandish experiments further prove the relevance of the science that is far better researched, performed, and peer-reviewed after publication in respected journals.

For while the world may have sped onward at a pace that our scientific contributions could not match, rendering our innovations lame and timid in comparison, I believe that my family's failure to make an impact on a world of the future is an important lesson. Our contributions must be remembered, not for their value to the progress of mankind, but for laying the foundations of the work that others would ignore because of other more viable innovations which they could hone to perfection.

The world may have progressed beyond a need for mad science, but I believe it is this spirit that will define my family's legacy. Even if what they did, does not.

Tipping the Scales

This is not a story of Icarian fate where rampant ambition overwhelms reason. No, it is a story of wartime oppression and dismissal by inbred monarchs who would blindly penalize neoteric enterprise instead of embracing the glory of modern advanced experimentation.

This is a story of three full generations of dedicated service by a proud Hungarian family with a rich history who were then flippantly cast out of their homes to live in exile. And for what? For revealing an uncomfortable truth? For showing that true science has the power to shape worlds and equally crush them within its grasp? My parents could not evade the royal scrutiny and here I exist, expatriated, wrenched from the work bequeathed to me.

Oh, how I wish I could view the well-kept estate of my youth with its comforting stone walls and ivy-laden iron gates. To gaze out of the northern veranda to the valley and watch the peasants wade through the smog like toads amongst the slough.
